works.abstract: Nonexhaust vehicle emissions (brake wear, tire wear, and road dust) now dominate particulate matter (PM) sources in urban environments as tailpipe emissions continue to decline. Among these, brake wear particles (BWPs) remain under-characterized, particularly their organic composition. This study investigates the formation and atmospheric relevance of amines released during the thermal degradation of phenolic resin, the primary binder in brake pads. Controlled brake dynamometer and phenolic-resin thermal degradation experiments were performed together with field measurements adjacent to two Southern California freeways (I-5, Santa Ana, and I-710, Long Beach). High-resolution mass spectrometry analysis revealed the prevalence of nitrogen-containing compounds across all data sets with dicyclohexylamine (C12H23N; DCHA) consistently detected in laboratory and ambient particles. DCHA concentrations in laboratory particles ranged from 0.08 to 1.6 ng/μg across brake pad types and resin conditions. DCHA was measured in air sampled onto filters at levels ranging from 2.1 ± 1.6 pg m–3 (Santa Ana) to 3.5 ± 1.7 pg m–3 (Long Beach). Ambient levels of DCHA correlated with near-road NO and brake-associated metals (Fe, Ba), suggesting a possible link between its emission and braking activity. These findings identify brake wear as a previously under-recognized source of DCHA and related organic nitrogen compounds, often associated primarily with tire wear emissions.
works.title: Laboratory and Field Investigation of Amines in Automotive Brake Wear Particles
